A single NOP instruction on x86 can be encoded in more than a dozen different byte sequences.
The Halting Problem was proven undecidable by Alan Turing in 1936, before electronic computers existed.
The first computer bug was an actual moth, found trapped in a Harvard Mark II relay in 1947.
x86 assembly still supports BCD arithmetic instructions from the 1970s that almost no modern compiler emits.
The C preprocessor has no concept of scope — #define is purely textual substitution.
Null-terminated strings exist because early C ran on machines where storing a length prefix cost real memory.
The term 'debugging' predates computers — Thomas Edison used it in an 1878 letter about electrical faults.
Some CPUs execute instructions out of order, then quietly discard the wrong branch's side effects — this exact behavior enabled Spectre.
IEEE 754 floating point has two zeros, +0 and -0, which compare equal but aren't bitwise identical.
The Y2038 problem exists because 32-bit Unix time overflows on January 19, 2038.
Rust's borrow checker is essentially a static analysis pass — there's no runtime cost once the program compiles.
The original UNIX was written in assembly, then rewritten in C specifically so it could be ported to other hardware.
Von Neumann architecture means code and data share the same memory space — part of why buffer overflows can execute as code.
The word 'byte' was coined at IBM in 1956, deliberately misspelled to avoid confusion with 'bit'.
A tail call, in principle, needs no new stack frame — some languages guarantee this optimization, most don't.
The first compiler, for A-0, was written by Grace Hopper in 1952.
ASCII only defines 128 characters because it was designed to fit in 7 bits, leaving the 8th bit free for parity checking.
The GIL in CPython exists because reference counting isn't atomic by default, not because Python 'can't do threads'.
Endianness gets its name from Gulliver's Travels, where a war breaks out over which end of an egg to crack.
Turing completeness only requires conditional branching and unbounded memory — the C++ template system qualifies.
The first hard disk drive, IBM's RAMAC in 1956, stored 5MB and weighed over a ton.
A hash collision doesn't mean broken data — it means two different inputs mapped to the same bucket, which is expected and handled.
The QWERTY layout wasn't designed to slow typists down — that's a popular myth; its real origins are still debated among historians.
Self-modifying code was common on early machines with no separate instruction cache to invalidate.
The stack grows downward in memory on most architectures purely by convention, not necessity.
Assembly mnemonics are not standardized — Intel and AT&T syntax write the same instruction with operands in reversed order.
The term 'garbage collection' was coined by John McCarthy for Lisp in 1959.
A segmentation fault doesn't mean you touched 'bad' memory — it means you touched memory the OS never mapped for your process.
Most 'random' number generators in standard libraries are deterministic pseudo-random generators seeded from a time or entropy source.
The first version of Unix time started at January 1, 1970, chosen arbitrarily as a round, recent epoch — not for any technical reason.
CPU cache lines are typically 64 bytes — false sharing bugs happen when two threads write to different variables that land in the same line.
